root_cause: Waves.update() calls this.spawn() on a 2000ms timer gated by `this.respawnPending > 0`, but spawn() itself already recursively schedules setTimeout(this.spawn,300) while decrementing respawnPending. Both the recursive setTimeout chain AND the update() timer draw from the same respawnPending counter, so the counter is decremented by two independent producers racing against each other. In headless QA the update-driven spawn (dt-clamped, min 2000ms) and the setTimeout-driven spawn can interleave harmlessly because timing is deterministic. In real browsers, two failure modes occur: (1) setTimeout throttling — Chrome/Brave/Firefox throttle or delay setTimeout callbacks in background/occluded tabs (and Brave's fingerprinting protection randomizes them), so the 300ms chain can be delayed long past a frame; meanwhile Waves.update() fires its own spawn every 2000ms of real time regardless, decrementing respawnPending faster than the setTimeout chain, so respawnPending hits 0 while the recursion chain is mid-flight. (2) Crucially, spawn() re-checks `if (this.respawnPending <= 0 || !this.active) return;` — if update() already drained respawnPending to 0, the pending setTimeout(this.spawn) callbacks silently return and the chain is abandoned; when a later wave calls start() it resets respawnPending to knightCount but the previous wave's orphaned setTimeout callbacks may fire after start(), each decrementing the new wave's respawnPending without adding proportional enemies, and eventually the new chain also returns early because a stale callback sees `this.current`/`this.active` mutated. Additionally waves.complete() is only triggered from Enemies.hurt when every enemy in list is dying, but dying enemies are spliced out of list in Enemies.update while rayTargets() filters them out — so if all enemies die, list may still contain dying entries and complete() is called repeatedly each hurt() after splice, causing multiple setTimeout(self.start,...) chains to be queued, each overwriting this.active and this.startTime and further desynchronizing respawnPending versus the actual live enemy count. Net effect: respawnPending drift to 0 while fewer than knightCount enemies exist, and update()'s 2000ms timer spawn silently no-ops because respawnPending is exhausted, so no more enemies ever appear — matching the 'waves active but nothing spawns' symptom in real browsers while headless passes.

The gun mesh is rotated `gun.rotation.set(0,0,Math.PI/2)` then `gun.rotation.y = Math.PI/2`. Euler order is XYZ, so the Z=+90° rotation is applied first, then Y=+90°. Quaternius revolver GLBs are modeled with the barrel along +X (the long axis of a pistol is the X axis in Blender-exported GLBs when the gun is laid flat) and the grip along -Y. After rotZ(+90°), the +X barrel maps to +Y (world up) and the -Y grip maps to +X (right). Then rotY(+90°) leaves +Y unchanged (Y is the rotation axis), so the barrel still points UP -> the defect (barrel aiming at the sky, grip to the right). To aim the muzzle along -Z, first bring the barrel from +X down to -Z: rotY(-90°) maps +X to +Z, but we want -Z, so rotY(+90°) maps +X to -Z. However that also rotates the grip. Better: apply a -90° rotation about Y to send barrel +X -> -Z, and a +90° rotation about Z to pivot the grip -Y -> -Z? No — grip must end up pointing downward (-Y). Pipe-line: v -> Rz(?) -> Ry(?). Solve so that (1,0,0) [barrel] -> (0,0,-1) and (0,-1,0) [grip] -> (0,-1,0). With XYZ order R = Ry * Rz (applied to vector as R v = Ry(Rz v)): fixed grip requires Rz(-Y)=z-axis-invariant => rotation must be about Y only, which cannot flip the barrel to -Z from +X *and* keep grip down simultaneously because Rz is needed to move the barrel from +X onto the Z axis. Actually Rz(90deg) sends +X->+Y then Ry(-90) sends +Y->+Y (unchanged), no. Use Rz(-90): +X->-Y, then Rx(-90): -Y->-Z. So final euler order XYZ with rx=-90, ry=0, rz=-90 sends barrel +X -> -Z (forward) and grip -Y -> -X? Let's verify: grip -Y under Rz(-90) -> -X; then Rx(-90) rotates Y,Z: -X is invariant -> -X (grip points left, wrong). Alternative Rz(+90): +X->+Y, then Rx(+90): +Y->+Z (barrel backward, wrong). The clean solution used by professional revolver rigs is to first rotate about Y to bring the +X barrel onto -Z (ry=+90), which also turns the grip from -Y toward the -Z->world? Actually rotations about Y leave the Y (vertical) axis fixed, so grip stays pointing -Y (down) — perfect. Then no Z rotation at all: rotate the model +90deg about Y: barrel +X->-Z (camera forward) and grip -Y stays -Y (down/right depending on lateral). To place the grip toward bottom-right (positive X, negative Y), add a small roll about Z of -0.35 rad and pitch about X of -0.1 rad for natural cant. So the corrected base euler is approximately (-0.1, Math.PI/2, -0.35). The original code's bug was stacking an unnecessary Z=+Math.PI/2 before the Y rotation, which pitched the barrel skyward because the prior Z rotation lifted the +X barrel onto +Y before the Y rotation (which cannot bring it back down).

When the player stands exactly on a collider center, d is 0 and the push direction falls back to (dx/(d||1), dz/(d||1)) = (0,0), so no separation occurs and the player remains pinned. Additionally, the per-frame full-penetration push removes the player's movement progress along the collision normal, which can make input appear to stick when repeatedly walking into a collider.
